newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish T-bill yields, zloty poised to rise.
newsitem.headline: Polish T-bill yields, zloty poised to rise.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields are expected to rise at Monday's one billion zloty primary auction in line with trends on the secondary market, analysts said on Friday.
They said the zloty was likely to eye further gains next week as the market keeps its bullish mentality and foreign investors pay for fixed bonds.
They said T-bills were not very attractive instruments for domestic banks who could buy higher-yielding NBP-bills, or for foreigners, who had to battle against a volatile exchange rate.

"Yields should rise several basis points for each maturity in small demand after foreign investor sales in secondary trade this week curbed the market's appetite," said Piotr Bednarek, senior T-bill dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Analysts said the zloty's gains against the currency basket late this week caused some shorter-term foreign investors to sell Polish paper before the next wave of central bank currency buying interventions would push the local unit down again.
At Monday's tender analysts expected demand to total about half of the offered amount, with nearly no foreign bids.
They said the average yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill to rise to 20.02 percent from 19.97 at this week's tender, while the 26-week yield to grow to 19.90 percent from 19.85.
The 13-week T-bill yield was expected to inch up slightly from last week's 19.60 percent with domestic corporates swallowing up most of the paper.
Analysts said foreigners, bullish on Poland's longer-term prospects, were more interested in longer instruments, such as the 12-percent five-year fixed bonds, than treasury bills.

"Such bonds are attractive to foreigners because Polish deficit spending (in the longer-term) is likely to be limited by a social security system overhaul and because the country's EMU aspirations will keep down the budget deficit," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

This week the new Finance Minister Marek Belka, whose nomination stirred no market reaction, vowed to speed up the overdue pension reform and said that a one-off zloty devaluation was not needed despite a growing trade deficit.

The zloty closed the week around 2.75 percent from the trading band centre versus last week's close at 2.36 percent after foreigners bought a majority of fixed bonds at Wednesday's 698 million zloty tender, payable next Wednesday.
Analysts said the zloty should nervously edge up toward resistance at 3.0 percent from parity next week amid expectations of a central bank intervention against the zloty.
"If the central bank does not purchase currencies (through an intervention) the zloty will strengthen next week," said Leszek Szafranek, forex dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
However, analysts were hard-pressed to explain the origin of the currency inflows which were expected to keep the zloty bullish after foreigners paid for fixed bonds.

"There is a natural trend to sell currencies, it may be caused by a combination of further foreign entry, relatively high (Polish) money market rates or investment inflows," said senior forex dealer at a foreign bank in Warsaw said.
One-day deposit rates on the money market closed on Friday around 22 percent, slightly higher than the central bank's main drainage rate of 21.64 percent for 14-days.
